summary: This memo answers the call in RFC 955 for a transaction-oriented protocol and continues the discussion of a possible transaction-oriented transport protocol. It does not propose a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 962 briefly considers adding TCP commands that would skip connection setup and close procedures for transaction traffic. The author explicitly says the idea is not a specification or standard proposal.

questions: what do nys and nif mean
did rfc 962 propose a tcp standard
subtitle: A brief discussion of skipping TCP setup and close steps for transaction traffic.

tldr.problem: The memo identifies connection setup and teardown time as a concern for transaction-oriented exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: It floats two possible TCP commands: NYS to avoid the handshake and NIF for a graceless close.
tldr.outcome: The author calls this a conceptual discussion rather than a specification and says the memo does not propose a standard.

today: RFC 962 is a discussion memo, not a proposed standard. It sketches NYS and NIF as possible additions to TCP without completing a specification.

sections.title: The Transaction-Oriented Question
sections.content:
The memo responds to a call for a transaction-oriented protocol. It identifies the time needed to set up and tear down a TCP connection as the perceived problem for a transaction.

The author assumes that other aspects of TCP's reliability and robustness would remain desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: A short request and reply may involve connection setup and teardown that take time. This memo considers whether those steps could be skipped.

sections.title: NYS and NIF Ideas
sections.content:
The author suggests adding NYS, meaning “no-way handshake,” and NIF, meaning “graceless close,” as TCP commands. The proposal would leave other aspects of TCP in place, apart from changing the version.

The memo notes that NYS would require careful handling of initial sequence numbers and retransmissions. It does not work out a complete procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: NYS would avoid the handshake, and NIF would avoid the ordinary close. The memo notes that sequence-number handling for NYS needs careful thought.

sections.title: Not a Specification
sections.content:
The author says the idea may conflict with the spirit of TCP and explicitly warns that the discussion should not be mistaken for a specification.

The memo continues discussion of a possible transaction-oriented transport protocol, without defining a complete protocol for implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC offers an idea to discuss, not a finished protocol. It does not ask readers to implement NYS or NIF.
